item.title: Ohio Gov. Issues Executive Order Challenging NCAA Eligibility Policy
item.dc:creator: Amanda Christovich
item.description: The EO may not have teeth, but it could still impact eligibility.
item.content:encoded:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine isn’t the first governor to weigh in on the eligibility battle being waged in college sports. But he is the first to issue an executive order on the subject.

On Tuesday, DeWine signed a three-page executive order stating that players who started college in 2022 and have exhausted four years of eligibility should be awarded a fifth year.

“No State institution of higher education or private college or university in Ohio shall uphold any rule, requirement, standard, or other limitation that prevents a student-athlete of that institution or college in the Class of 2022 from fully participating in intercollegiate athletics in the 2026-27 academic year,” the order states. The only caveats: Players must still be 24 or younger (in keeping with the NCAA’s age-based policy), must be academically eligible, and cannot have signed professional contracts.

The executive order comes as multiple cases at the state and federal level have challenged the implementation of the NCAA’s age-based eligibility policy, which went into effect this summer. The new rule allows players five years to complete up to five seasons of eligibility, beginning on their 19th birthday or when they start college, whichever comes first. But the NCAA decided that the rule doesn’t retroactively apply to the freshman class of 2022. Over the past several months, hundreds of players in that 2022 class have filed lawsuits to win back a fifth year.

The order also comes as the U.S. House of Representatives gears up to consider the Protect College Sports Act, which would codify the NCAA’s new policy into federal law. The new law would not, however, cancel out previous eligibility cases filed before it was signed.

Now, Gov. DeWine has tried to create some consistency—at least for players at Ohio schools. 

The immediate effects of the executive order are unclear, however. 

The EO “doesn’t require those schools to roster the players, but provides them cover if they choose to,” sports attorney Darren Heitner tells FOS. However, the EO itself may not have the power to “supercede” NCAA rules.

“This EO only has legal teeth if the schools think that it has legal teeth,” Boise State sports law professor Sam Ehrlich tells FOS. “From there, things get complicated. I think there are several legal theories that the NCAA could use to attack this if needed.” 

Nebraska attorney general Mike Hilgers also questioned the order’s enforceability. “I can’t imagine such an order being enforceable across the league, let alone in Nebraska,” he said. “Either way, our office is reviewing this very closely as it appears contrary to every rule currently in place.”

The NCAA has already taken this position. On Tuesday night, NCAA president Charlie Baker said in a memo to schools that the organization intends to continue enforcing eligibility rules “consistently,” including in Ohio. 

“The Governor of Ohio cannot legislate NCAA eligibility rules,” Baker wrote. “One elected official seeking to make their own rules for their own schools’ advantage is a terrible way to run athletic competitions and precisely why Congress must pass the PCSA [Protect College Sports Act] as soon as possible.” 

But the document could help sway Ohio’s supreme court toward the players’ position when it reviews Borovicanin v. NCAA, the first case filed on this issue, which counts dozens of men’s and women’s basketball players as plaintiffs. (Players initially won eligibility, but their injunction was overturned on appeal.)

“It’s a fairly strong statement of policy,” Seton Hall law professor Bob Boland tells FOS. However, he noted the EO includes a potentially complicating provision: “Nothing in this Order is intended to decide, or to direct any court considering any matter pending before any court, or to require any institution to act contrary to an order of a court of competent jurisdiction.”

Ultimately, though, the order could have a ripple effect nationwide, legal experts said. The EO could also be emulated by other state governors who may want their state universities to have the competitive advantage offered by these players looking for eligibility. Though one executive order in one state may not technically have teeth, the NCAA may have a harder time fighting multiple state governors.

The post Ohio Gov. Issues Executive Order Challenging NCAA Eligibility Policy appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Pablo Torre: More Coming on Clippers, Life Surge … and LeBron?
item.dc:creator: Colin Salao
item.description: LeBron’s relationship with Fanatics allows him to use its helicopter.
item.content:encoded:
Pablo Torre says he has more to report on his recent major investigations on the Clippers and Kawhi Leonard, and Life Surge.

Speaking Tuesday at the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit, Torre said there’s still “plenty” to share on the Clippers and Leonard, including about Lockton Insurance, a fourth sponsor tied to Leonard. He also mentioned Rhode Island Football Club, a USL team Leonard and his uncle Dennis Robertson invested in, according to his reporting.

“That was not even vaguely referred to in the report, and we’ve done reporting on that,” Torre said, referring to the report published in September by an independent law firm hired by the NBA to investigate the Clippers for violating the league’s cap circumvention rules. 

The NBA imposed significant penalties on the Clippers and several executives following the law firm’s report. Torre first started investigating potential cap circumvention by the Clippers on his podcast, Pablo Torre Finds Out, nearly a year earlier. Torre has since published more than a dozen podcasts reporting on the Clippers and Leonard.

The U.S. Department of Justice is also reportedly investigating.

As for Life Surge, a faith-based, for-profit, wealth-building and motivational organization, Torre published his first podcast in late September alleging the group is misleading people into ponying up thousands of dollars with the help of sports stars, including Tim Tebow and Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla. 

Torre said that like Leonard and the Clippers, the investigation on Life Surge will be a “series.”

“We will have a follow-up,” Torre said. “We’re doing reporting about all of this, and I’m excited to tell people as we continue to vet our own work and fact-check that I think there’s a lot more that will open people’s eyes.”

Since Torre’s report, multiple sports figures have distanced themselves from Life Surge, including Tebow.

“The allegations are extremely, extremely serious and it’s something that we take very serious,” Tebow said a day after Torre’s podcast episode was published. “And so for us, we’re having our team do an investigation but also pausing our relationship until we can learn more about the facts to be able to understand more.” 

LeBron Investigation Coming?

Torre also discussed his interest in the ties between LeBron James and Fanatics, particularly the helicopter James uses to fly back and forth between Philadelphia and New York while playing for the Sixers. FOS reported last week that James can use Fanatics’s aviation for free as a part of the deal he signed with the company in 2024, when he was still on the Lakers.

“I will say that we’re very interested, and we are, of course, looking into all of the way that is both a good story, as well as something that’s of interest to the league,” Torre said. 

Torre added he’s received messages from NBA owners asking him to explain James’s deal, but didn’t say whether he will actually publish anything on the matter.

The post Pablo Torre: More Coming on Clippers, Life Surge … and LeBron? appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: ESPN Exec Mike Foss: Pat McAfee ‘Might Be a Journalist At Heart’
item.dc:creator: Eli Kronenberg
item.description: Foss said he had “absolutely nothing” to say to McAfee’s critics.
item.content:encoded:
New ESPN executive vice president Mike Foss defended Pat McAfee’s ever-growing role at the network, calling McAfee a “generational” talent.

“It’s funny, I think he might be a journalist at heart,” Foss said while speaking at the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit in New York. “I think what you find as he puts the show together each day and something piques his interest, he’s got the rolodex, so he … has built access that a lot of people don’t have the ability to do.”

Asked what he would say to critics of McAfee’s College GameDay antics, Foss was blunt. “Absolutely nothing,” Foss told FOS’s Mike McCarthy. 

Foss joined ESPN in 2017 as a senior vice president after spending time at Fox Sports and USA Today. This May, he was promoted to the title of “Executive Vice President, Executive Editor, Sports News and Entertainment,” succeeding the retiring Dave Roberts. 

Foss also commented on the return of McAfee’s popular field goal kicking contest in which fans have the opportunity to earn $1 million by making a 33-yard field goal live on College GameDay. McAfee had cast some doubt on whether the contest would return this season, but Foss said he didn’t believe it was ever at risk.

“I don’t know if he was ever undecided, I think he might’ve done a little theater,” Foss said. “Especially given how much he’s donated this year, I don’t think you give away $12 million just on a whim.”

McAfee joined College GameDay as a full-time analyst in 2022 after his podcast, The Pat McAfee Show, exploded in popularity. ESPN began licensing The Pat McAfee Show in 2023, though McAfee still owns the intellectual property.

College GameDay has broken its own viewership records multiple times in recent years. It is currently averaging 2.8 million viewers at the midpoint of the 2026 college football season, putting this year on track to be the most-watched in the show’s history.

On Tuesday, McAfee poured cold water over McCarthy’s recent opinion column suggesting he could soon land on the Monday Night Football broadcast, writing on X, “This isn’t real. There’s been zero conversation about this.”

Asked whether he could envision McAfee commentating on MNF games, Foss stressed the job was not currently available due to Joe Buck and Troy Aikman’s presence in the booth, but added that McAfee’s upcoming Super Bowl alt-cast was evidence of his growing star power. 

“Pat can do whatever he wants,” Foss said. “If Pat wants to call football games full-time, that’s a decision that he’s gonna make, and I would never bet against him.”

The post ESPN Exec Mike Foss: Pat McAfee ‘Might Be a Journalist At Heart’ appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Elle Duncan: WNBA Culture Wars Are ‘Open Season’ on Black Women
item.dc:creator: Yanyan Li
item.description: Duncan reiterated her belief that covering the league is “toxic as hell.”
item.content:encoded:
Netflix and USA Sports anchor Elle Duncan believes that the WNBA has become a hotbed for culture wars because the league has a “large faction of” Black and queer players.

“It feels like open season to dunk on Black women because we do not have protection. Because no one cares. Because we are low-hanging fruit,” Duncan told Baker Machado at Front Office Sports’s Tuned In summit on Tuesday. “Because it is very easy to dunk on us since we are, I would say, outside of transgender people, the most marginalized of the marginalized groups.”

Duncan is the lead studio host for USA Network’s WNBA coverage. She also covered the WNBA when she worked at ESPN, prior to leaving the company in December 2025 for Netflix and USA Network.

Duncan called covering the league “toxic as hell,” blaming “opportunists” who want to criticize Black and queer women, while uplifting “one person” who they “see in their own image.” Her sentiment has been a talking point in the WNBA since Caitlin Clark was drafted in 2024 and significantly boosted the league’s popularity, sparking several conversations related to how Clark is discussed in relation to Black and queer players.

Since Clark joined the WNBA, several Black players have spoken about the racism they’ve received following on-court incidents with the Indiana Fever guard. 

Following a playoff series between the Fever and the Connecticut Sun in 2024, former Connecticut Sun guard DiJonai Carrington shared an email she received with a racial slur and sexual assault threats, while her then-teammate Alyssa Thomas called out the Fever fans behind the “racial comments” she’s received. Thomas also said in June that she received “threats against her life” after receiving a one-game suspension for a foul on Clark.

“It’s twofold for them—so you get to lift this one person up, and you get to, ultimately, reduce everybody else that isn’t her to nothing,” Duncan said.

In the 2026 season, Clark’s Indiana Fever teammate Sophie Cunningham has been the primary lightning rod for WNBA culture wars. After saying in a July ESPN article that she wanted to protect “young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” she sparked a widespread firestorm—which included the increased presence of advocates against transgender women in women’s sports at WNBA games, as well as former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White publicly declaring for the league’s draft and attending games.

Duncan said that the racism toward Black WNBA players is also directed toward members of the media like herself, and is a representation of what Black women face in society. She said she gets told that she’s a “DEI hire,” a sentiment which she believes minimizes her efforts in her work.

“It’s frustrating to talk about because I know this is going to get clipped. This is going to be me saying goodbye to my mentions for the next couple of days,” Duncan said. “But it’s going to be me lamenting that being a Black woman is so hard, and someone’s going to tweet at me that I work at Netflix and I’m fine and I don’t have any struggles in my life. And it’s just this constant cycle where we’re getting nowhere and no one is listening to anybody.”

While Duncan acknowledges the difficulties of engaging in a “toxic” WNBA social media landscape, she believes that fixing it comes with continued support for the league’s players to “get these bad-faith characters out of here.”

Choosing the next WNBA commissioner

Duncan also called for the WNBA’s next commissioner to help battle divisiveness, while simultaneously being a bridge between players and owners. She believes that current commissioner Cathy Engelbert, who is set to retire after the 2026 season, has not done a good job at the latter.

“The goal of the next commissioner should be twofold. The first thing is figuring out how we work on this divisiveness, how we wrestle the narrative back. The second thing would be connecting the players and owners,” Duncan said. “If there’s criticism of Cathy, it’s been that some commissioners are player-friendly, and some commissioners are very team-friendly, and maybe Cathy is neither.”

Duncan reinforces the point that has been made by several WNBA players. Reigning MVP A’ja Wilson said in July that her only relationship with Engelbert is when the commissioner hands her awards.

While Duncan believes that WNBA team owners would not want a former player as commissioner, she says that she wants someone with “at least a background in basketball” to be in charge of the league next.

The post Elle Duncan: WNBA Culture Wars Are ‘Open Season’ on Black Women appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: LPGA Commissioner: Good Good Driver Ad ‘Brutal’ Situation
item.dc:creator: David Rumsey
item.description: Kessler said people should be allowed to make mistakes and ask for forgiveness.
item.content:encoded:
LPGA commissioner Craig Kessler called the now-infamous Good Good Golf–Callaway driver ad a “brutal” and “heartbreaking” situation, but said people should still be able to seek forgiveness for making mistakes.

“In many ways, heartbreaking,” Kessler said when asked about the topic during the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit Tuesday. “The fact that someone thought that was a good idea, and it came to life, just shows you that while society has made enormous progress, we have a very, very long way to go.”

Good Good has been trying to get back to business as usual, nearly two months removed from losing its partnership with Callaway, dropping its sponsorship of a new PGA Tour event, having its merchandise pulled from many stores, and seeing its reality TV competition series on Golf Channel get cancelled.

The LPGA did not have any official partnership with Good Good. And while not defending Good Good’s handling of the situation, Kessler said, “Good people make mistakes, and we have to leave room in society for someone to say, ‘I made a massive mistake. Please forgive me. Here’s what I learned, and it won’t happen again.’”

Kessler brought up a controversy of his own from back in February when he ultimately issued a public apology for his decision to cancel the final round of the LPGA’s season-opening tournament amid freezing temperatures in Florida.

“I got vilified for making that call,” Kessler said. “I mean, vilified. My kids came home from elementary school, and they’re like, ‘Dad, my friend Googled you, and it seems like you suck at your job.’” Kessler said his biggest regret was overruling several of his team members in making the decision. 

“They were right, and I was wrong,” Kessler said. “Should I have lost my job for making a mistake? Like, that’s crazy. If we live in this world where every single time somebody makes a mistake, there’s no chance to learn from it and ask for forgiveness, I don’t know how we’re ever going to raise a society of risk takers.”

Ultimately, Kessler said of the Good Good situation, “Brutal that it happened—awful—my heart goes out to anybody who was affected, and I think a lot of lessons were learned.”

LPGA’s Executive Movement

Last month, Chad Coleman stepped down as the LPGA’s chief marketing officer just eight months after taking the job. He was previously the CEO of Dude Perfect, and a widely praised hire—one of the first of Kessler’s tenure that only began in May 2025.

“I have a lot of love and respect for Chad,” Kessler said Tuesday. “He’s a wonderful husband, father of two beautiful girls, and wherever Chad ends up next, that organization will be lucky to have him.” Coleman has signaled that he has another job lined up but has not publicly announced his next move.

Kessler added that beyond Coleman’s departure, several other recent hires “have absolutely changed the trajectory of the LPGA,” like VP of strategy Aliea Clark, chief sales and partnerships officer Monica Fee (a former LIV Golf executive), and chief administrative officer Casey Daniel.

The post LPGA Commissioner: Good Good Driver Ad ‘Brutal’ Situation appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Chris Berman: Damar Hamlin’s Cardiac Arrest Slowed NFL’s 18-Game Push
item.dc:creator: Yanyan Li and Mark Maske
item.description: The NFL declined to comment on Berman’s comments.
item.content:encoded:
Longtime ESPN commentator Chris Berman says he believes Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin’s on-field cardiac arrest in 2023 slowed an NFL push for an 18-game regular season.

“The push that might have happened while these current deals were in place—once Damar Hamlin happened, not the time to put it forward,” Berman said on Tuesday at Front Office Sports’ Tuned In summit. “That’s my belief. I’m sure I’m not too far off.”

In January 2023, Hamlin suffered cardiac arrest after making a tackle during a Bills-Bengals game, an incident that sparked widespread conversation about player safety across the league.

The NFL declined an FOS request for comment. ESPN declined to comment on the matter. 

Under its current collective bargaining agreement (CBA), which was approved in 2020 and runs until 2030, the NFL cannot feasibly extend to an 18-game season. That CBA allowed the NFL to expand from a 16- to a 17-game season, which the league did in 2021, but it does not permit extending the season to 18 games.

However, the issue has been a long-time talking point—the NFL and its owners proposed an 18-game season as far back as the negotiations that led to the 2011 CBA. 

Owners and the league have expressed interest in implementing an 18-game season, and want to discuss it as part of the upcoming negotiations on the next CBA, and had informal talks with the NFLPA on the issue under former executive director Lloyd Howell Jr. Howell resigned in July 2025, and JC Tretter was elected as his replacement this March; formal negotiations on the 18-game season and other CBA issues have remained on hold.

In February, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said expanding to 18 games was “not a given” and that player safety concerns would be a consideration in the next CBA negotiations. David White, the NFLPA’s interim executive director between Howell and Tretter’s tenures, said in February that players “don’t have an appetite” for an 18th game.

Berman believes the 18-game push is now resurfacing because the current CBA and league media rights deal are moving into their final years. (The NFL can opt out of its TV contracts as early as 2030.)

“When the NFL floats stuff, it’s not a done deal by any means, but it’s a bigger magnitude than what I’m going to say,” Berman said. “The NFL is smarter than everybody else. You didn’t hear anything about it for a couple years because you’d have to get the players and everyone [to approve], and then maybe with three years left in this TV deal, ‘Yeah, we’re having 18 games.’”

The post Chris Berman: Damar Hamlin’s Cardiac Arrest Slowed NFL’s 18-Game Push appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: PTPA Boss Accused of Harassment, Sexist Conduct in New Lawsuit
item.dc:creator: Daniel Kaplan
item.description: The PTPA is listed as both a plaintiff and a defendant.
item.content:encoded:
The drama surrounding the Professional Tennis Players Association added a new chapter today, with the organization’s controversially ousted general counsel suing the current and past executive directors in a six-count lawsuit alleging breaches of fiduciary duty. 

Underscoring just how bizarre the civil war at the group is, the PTPA is listed as both a plaintiff and a defendant.

The 76-page case, filed in Cook County Circuit Court in Illinois, recaps some of what is already known about the civil war at the pro tennis players’ advocacy group. Wajid Mir, the former general counsel, argued he and others were waging a battle for transparency within the organization when he was fired—illegitimately he claims—by those who were allegedly trying to cover up their misdeeds. Much of this is ground covered in previous and ongoing litigation, but this new lawsuit has some fresh, highly charged claims about the former executive director, Ahmad Nassar, and his successor, Romain Rosenberg.

After complaints were leveled at Nassar that his dual roles running the PTPA and its commercial operator, Winners Alliance, conflicted, he stepped down in March in favor of Rosenberg. The move came shortly after cofounder Novak Djokovic stepped away from the PTPA.

Nassar left to focus solely on Winners Alliance, which is in part backed by billionaire investor Bill Ackman. In early June, Mir assembled six players who he said were approved as board members to hear a complaint that Rosenberg had harassed PTPA employee Anastasia Skavronskaia, who was formerly a marketing agent for Martina Hingis. 

“The Committee unanimously voted 6–0 to remove Rosenberg from executive authority effective immediately due to ‘misogynistic’ conduct, harassment and workplace retaliation,” Mir claims in the lawsuit. 

Rosenberg did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Rosenberg held an alternate committee meeting the next day with different players, sidestepping the previous day’s action, and his board members agreed to fire Mir. As Rosenberg is connected to Nassar and Winners Alliance, that side controlled the group’s purse strings and human resources, leaving him in charge.  

The players on the earlier committee sued in Washington, D.C., circuit court, but soon ran out of money; the judge also declined to enjoin the Rosenberg-led board. That judge also said each board was likely not viable because of eligibility restrictions.

The PTPA then sued Mir in Illinois federal court. Mir, who resides in Illinois, filed today a separate case known as a derivative claim, which is a lawsuit brought by an interested party.

In it, he claims Nassar is still effectively running the PTPA, which doesn’t appear to have many, if any, employees outside of Rosenberg. Skavronskaia was let go after the US Open ended in September. 

Nassar launched Winners Alliance in 2022 to be the commercial agent for the tennis players organization, which had recently hired Nassar away from the NFLPA. 

Winners Alliance made several other sports investments, including notorious track start-up Grand Slam Track, which recently exited Chapter 11 bankruptcy. For the PTPA, Winners Alliance signed a term sheet to pay the group $3 million a year for 20 years in return for the rights to market player group licensing rights.  Mir claims the term sheet was approved by the board but never fully signed, meaning Winners Alliance could end the partnership.

Outside of the internal legal battle, the PTPA is perhaps best known for its antitrust lawsuit against both tennis tours and three Grand Slams, a case that recently survived a motion to dismiss. Outside of that, the PTPA—founded in 2020—has made little impact in tennis. When Djokovic separated from the group in January, he cited transparency issues, and Mir had been trying to woo him back until events exploded in June.  

Mir alleges Nassar remains conflicted about whether his duties are to PTPA or Winners Alliance. And he claims a new conflict may have emerged with what he says in the lawsuit is Nassar’s creation of a firm for Muslim athletes called Companions Alliance. 

“It remains unclear what, if any, capital or operational resources Nassar and/or Winners Alliance have allocated to Companions Alliance,” the lawsuit reads. “These facts warrant examination of the source, structure, authorization, and organizational relationship of such expenditures and activities.”

In a statement to Front Office Sports, Nassar said, “This complaint was filed by a former PTPA staff member who was terminated in June and whom the PTPA and Winners Alliance are already suing in federal court. It recycles governance arguments the D.C. Superior Court did not accept, and he has no standing to bring claims on the PTPA’s behalf. I am about to begin a planned medical leave for major surgery related to a serious diagnosis, and our counsel will respond forcefully in court.”

Mir also charges the PTPA worked with, and employed Mohammed Tarik Koubaa, who led PTPA Global Services in Dubai. According to the lawsuit, Koubaa had “become the subject of serious workplace concerns. Rosenberg and Skavornskaia were made aware of concerns regarding comments by Koubaa toward players who identify as LGBTQ, with players informing Rosenberg in 2025 and 2026 that they would refuse to attend PTPA events if Koubaa were present.”

Skavornskaia also claimed Koubaa sexually harassed her at the Australian Open in 2025.

And Mir takes aim at Djokovic’s partner in forming the PTPA, the recently retired Vasek Pospisil and the named plaintiff in the antitrust case. “PTPA and Winners Alliance represented that payments to players associated with PTPA governance could involve activities characterized as outside PTPA business,” the suit says. “Pospisil was paid over $600,000 through 2025 and retains over $2 million of Winners Alliance equity.”

The post PTPA Boss Accused of Harassment, Sexist Conduct in New Lawsuit appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Michael Jordan Is ‘All In’ on Racing After Legal Fight: NASCAR CEO
item.dc:creator: Eric Fisher
item.description: The NASCAR CEO said the Bulls legend is a "true fan.”
item.content:encoded:
While the basketball world laments the absence of Michael Jordan from the sport, NASCAR is reveling in the icon’s deepening motorsports involvement. 

NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell said at the Front Office Sports Tuned In media summit Tuesday that Jordan, the co-owner of 23XI Racing, is “all in” about the future of racing. 

“He shows up at every race. He’s passionate about the sport, and for NASCAR, you can’t pay for that,” O’Donnell said about Jordan. “You can bring celebrities or athletes to the race who may or may not be [racing] fans, but he’s a true fan, and he cares about the sport.” 

That sentiment highlights a vast difference from nearly a year ago, when NASCAR and Jordan were locked in a bitter antitrust legal fight. As a high-stakes trial began last December in Charlotte, the two sides, along with Front Row Motorsports, reached a surprise settlement that included the creation of evergreen charters that guarantee teams race entry and a larger share of purse money.

“Being in a courtroom, looking across and seeing Michael Jordan was just a little bit odd,” O’Donnell said. “But even during that time, and at the end of that trial, we had a discussion about the fact that he was all in, and so are we.”

The current alignment between NASCAR and Jordan differs strongly from basketball, where the former Bulls superstar and then Wizards executive and Hornets owner had a highly limited guest role on NBC Sports last season—one that likely isn’t being reprised for the 2026–27 NBA campaign starting next week.

“Even during the NBA All-Star Game, Michael was with us at a NASCAR race. That shows his passion,” O’Donnell said. “He’s invested in the sport, he’s a winner, and he wants to see his team win, so we’re excited to have him.”

Despite all that, NBC Sports is still defending what it did last season with Jordan.

“I love the fact that we did one interview—and you can say what you want about it airing once or being spread out over our series of pregame shows during the year—it’s a year later and people are still talking about it,” NBC Sports announcer Mike Tirico said at Tuned In. 

O’Donnell has also reached a level of rapport with Jordan that MLS commissioner Don Garber is attempting to forge with soccer icon Lionel Messi. 

The NASCAR antitrust fight was just one of several major organizational changes over the past year that also included the departure of former commissioner Steve Phelps, as well as former CEO Jim France, part of NASCAR’s controlling family, relinquishing that title. O’Donnell said the NASCAR commissioner title is not likely to be refilled.

“For us, I think we’ll leave it where it is,” O’Donnell said regarding NASCAR’s leadership hierarchy. “If you look at our sport, we’re different, and looking forward, I don’t expect us to have a commissioner. The job right now is to go out with all the different stakeholders, bring them together, and make some tough decisions. But we’re going to be a lot faster about what we do in terms of making decisions, smart ones, but really getting folks pivoted toward what is the art of the possible.”

Hollywood Lift

NASCAR, meanwhile, is eagerly awaiting the planned 2028 release of the sequel to Days Of Thunder, the 1990 motorsports movie starring Tom Cruise. The original Days of Thunder helped lead NASCAR into a golden age that decade, and a similar lift is anticipated this time around.

Far from being a passive observer, NASCAR is actively involved in the movie’s production, including supplying more than 80 race cars that will be involved in the filming. 

“Tom’s message to us was, ‘I’m going to put you in front of an entirely new audience,’” O’Donnell said. “So for us, it’s obviously a whole new open door…He wants this to be as authentic as it can be. We’ll see how the storylines come together, but we’re producing probably more than 80 cars that are going to be part of this. Some we don’t expect to get back as they’re wrecked as part of this. But this is absolutely a big opportunity for us across the board.”

The post Michael Jordan Is ‘All In’ on Racing After Legal Fight: NASCAR CEO appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Taylor Rooks Defends Friendships With Athletes She Covers
item.dc:creator: Ben Horney
item.description: “I actually think it sometimes might make it a little bit easier.”
item.content:encoded:
Taylor Rooks is unapologetic about the close friendships she’s built with the athletes she covers.

This summer, the host of Amazon Prime Video’s NBA on Prime attended the weddings of NBA stars Tyrese Haliburton and Donovan Mitchell on back to back days, she told Bridget Condon during the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit on Tuesday. Kevin Durant is also a “close friend,” she said—he attended her wedding last year, and she’s an equity partner in his company, Boardroom, she said.

Rooks doesn’t believe those relationships compromise her work; if anything, they can make it easier to have difficult conversations.

“I actually think it sometimes might make it a little bit easier,” she said. “Largely because a lot of those tough conversations, you’re just having already.”

For example, she said during Mitchell’s wedding she had a discussion with the Cavaliers star about why he hasn’t been able to get his team over the hump. Although Mitchell has had a stellar career, including seven All-Star appearances, he’s only made the conference finals once, last season, when his team was swept by the Knicks.  “What is it about your play?” she said she asked him. “Are you not elevating your teammates?”

Having private conversations about topics like that makes it easier for her to ask hard questions when she’s sitting down for a televised one-on-one, Rooks said.

“It’s about honesty,” she told FOS. “Those questions are fair. Your story is your story.”

She doesn’t worry about breaking the trust of a close friend who is also an athlete she covers. “I think that one of the reasons you end up sitting with me is because there is the trust that exists,” she said. “And that trust really is this daily deposit, both with the audience and with the person that you’re interviewing.”

Her friendship with Durant dates back years. Rooks said that she first met Durant when she was a sophomore in college and traveled to Florida to cover the All-Star Game. 

“KD sees this little girl running around trying to get people to answer her questions,” she said. “He said, ‘you can ask me.’ It was my first big interview.”

Nowadays, Rooks considers Durant a “close friend,” but that hasn’t stopped her from asking him tough questions on camera. “We have done tons of interviews, some that were exclusives,” she said. 

Reporters getting too close with the people they cover can lead to backlash, especially for female reporters who are often scrutinized differently than their male counterparts. She previously addressed that in a 2025 Substack post, writing there are people who feel she “should change my personal relationships with athletes simply because I’m a woman (despite the fact that male reporters have built their entire careers on access and relationships).” She doubled down on that point during Tuned In.

“This is a relationship business,” she said. “This is about maintaining relationships, building relationships.”

Rooks is able to remain level-headed thanks, in part, to a simple rule she’s been living by for years: Ignore the online critics.

“I let go of online criticism a long time ago,” she told FOS. People who go online to criticize me… It doesn’t register with me. Because I know what’s true about my life, my credibility, my profession.”

The post Taylor Rooks Defends Friendships With Athletes She Covers appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: MLS Not Looking Into NYCFC Owners Over Manchester City Violations
item.dc:creator: Eli Kronenberg
item.description: Manchester City was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.
item.content:encoded:
MLS commissioner Don Garber suggested the league was unlikely to investigate New York City FC’s Abu Dhabi-based majority owners, who have been implicated in Manchester City’s guilty verdict for breaching Premier League financial regulations. 

“We’re not in the business of looking [at] what our team owners do in other leagues,” Garber said while speaking at the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit in New York. “And frankly, I don’t think any league would view what other owners do when they have multiple investments throughout other sports.”

NYCFC and Manchester City are both owned by City Football Group, a holding company run by Abu Dhabi royal family member Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan. 

In late September, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found Manchester City guilty of serious financial breaches. The league said that, between 2009 and 2018, City artificially inflated its revenue and reduced its costs by more than 900 million pounds by entering into “sham” sponsorship contracts that were partially funded by the club’s owners. 

Misrepresenting its revenue and costs allowed City to skirt the league’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules, which limited how much money a club could lose over a rolling three-year period. City is appealing the verdict. 

Mansour bought City in 2008, and he and club CEO Ferran Soriano founded City Football Group in 2013 with the vision of adding clubs around the globe to the club’s ownership portfolio, starting with NYCFC. In May 2013, City joined forces with the Yankees to launch NYCFC as an MLS expansion team. 

The New York outfit was branded nearly identically to its parent club, with the same sky-blue home kit and primary shirt sponsor, Etihad Airways. 

The two clubs coordinated multiple player transfers in NYCFC’s early years. Frank Lampard was announced as one of NYCFC’s first signings in 2014, joining from Chelsea. But after it later emerged that he had never signed an MLS contract, City used him for a season before he settled on American soil, upsetting some fans of the nascent New York franchise.

City Football Group holds an 80% stake in NYCFC, while Yankee Global Enterprises and businessman Marcelo Claure each own 10%. 

NYCFC is set to open Etihad Park, a new 25,000-seat stadium, next July. The stadium site in Queens is adjacent to Citi Field and the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, and it will be the city’s first soccer-specific stadium.

At Tuned In, Garber praised City Football Group for its investment in the club.

“What NYCFC has done through their ownership, the City Football Group, in investing in our league, building a great team in NYCFC, building an MLS Next Pro Stadium in New Jersey, and obviously their stadium that’ll open up in Queens, is something we’re thankful for and appreciative of,” Garber said.

The post MLS Not Looking Into NYCFC Owners Over Manchester City Violations appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Jessica Berman Says It’s ‘My Job’ to Solve NWSL Louisville Problem
item.dc:creator: Margaret Fleming
item.description: Louisville falling behind “shows you how quickly this league has changed.”
item.content:encoded:
As the NWSL regular season winds down, Racing Louisville and its fans sit in limbo waiting to find out about the team’s future amid a possible relocation to Cincinnati.

NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman is ready to find a solution for the five-year-old club.

“In order to keep up with the demands and expectations of our league, there is an expectation that is not in any way rationally related to the expectations that existed five years ago,” Berman said at the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit  on Tuesday.

“So it’s our job, it’s my job, to work with them to find solutions that can make sure that we respect our incumbent owners and solve for making sure that the club and the team are set up for success moving forward.”

Following an ESPN report earlier this year that the team was exploring selling ownership stakes, the chair of Racing Louisville’s ownership group, John Neace, told local business and political leaders in August that the club “will be forced to do something” if its poor attendance does not improve.

Last month, ESPN reported that the owners of MLS side FC Cincinnati engaged in talks to relocate Racing Louisville.

Racing Louisville’s ownership group, Soccer Holdings, also owns the men’s second-division team Louisville City FC. The two teams share training facilities and 15,000-person Lynn Family Stadium downtown. Racing Louisville has made the playoffs only once since joining the NWSL in 2021.

Soccer Holdings paid roughly $1 million to $2 million as an expansion fee. A half-decade later, the NWSL’s newest owners, the billionaire Haslam family in Columbus, paid a $205 million expansion fee.

“When they invested in this league, I think it’s not an overstatement to say that it was a completely different value proposition and investment thesis and expectations for capital,” Berman said.

Berman noted Louisville’s facilities, saying she was “amazed” on her first site visit after becoming commissioner in 2022. “At that time, Louisville was actually the leader in our league for infrastructure, and that just shows you how quickly this league has changed.”

Possible Team in Cincinnati

The NWSL expanded to 16 teams this season with Boston and Denver, and will grow to 18 teams in 2028 with the addition of Atlanta and Columbus.

Expansion isn’t slowing down anytime soon, with Berman saying the league is in “active conversations” with markets who want to become the 19th and 20th teams.

The NWSL recently passed over Cincinnati as an expansion market. Caitlin Clark was involved in the bid, but a representative for the WNBA star did not confirm if she would be involved with a potential relocation team.

“Cincinnati would be an example of an MLS owner who has proven that they can operate a best-in-class organization in another league,” Berman said, “and [the NWSL is] certainly excited to continue to discuss with them and others like them who are either shared resource or independent who we feel like could add value to our league both from a business perspective, a sporting perspective, and an ownership perspective.”

The post Jessica Berman Says It’s ‘My Job’ to Solve NWSL Louisville Problem appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: How a Lunch in Atlanta Led to Josh Pate’s ESPN College Football Show
item.dc:creator: Amanda Christovich
item.description: Pate told ESPN that legacy media was underserving college football fans.
item.content:encoded:
College football analyst and personality Josh Pate is amid his inaugural season hosting a weekly traveling ESPN college football show, Bussin’ and Pate on Campus, alongside Bussin’ With the Boys cohosts Will Compton and Taylor Lewan. 

The show is more than just the next step for Pate’s relationship with ESPN after he appeared regularly on multiple network shows last season. It’s a sign of the network’s major investment into college football programming, outside game-day broadcasts.

It all started with lunch in Atlanta on the eve of last year’s SEC Conference Championship Game with Pate, ESPN president of content Burke Magnus, and a few other executives. At the time, Pate was a regular contributor to multiple ESPN morning shows, like Get Up and First Take, in addition to his YouTube college football show. But he didn’t have his own independent content with ESPN—at least not yet.

“[Magnus] was really inquisitive, which kind of surprised me. He really wanted to know, ‘what do you think? What do you think about college football?,’” Pate told Ryan Glasspiegel at the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit on Tuesday. “Just dealing with high-level media executives, that hasn’t been my experience. My experience has normally been, index finger in your face, so to speak.” 

Pate joked that he asked Magnus if he had “permission to speak freely,” which Magnus granted.

“My opinion had been for a while, dating back years and years and years, that just the overall legacy media system had underserved college football,” Pate told Glasspiegel. “From a broadcasting of game perspective, it’s immaculate, it looks incredible. But from the Sunday through Friday perspective, I’m looking at 37 different NBA shows on networks and there’s really not one college football studio show post-Rece Davis, Mark May, Lou Holtz College Football Live era that’s speaking to me. I’m having to go elsewhere for it.”

This belief, Pate said, was the “impetus” for the college football show he created. “Even all these years later, with all the nine- and ten-figures invested in media rights, I thought it was still underserved,” he said. “So I shared that. And [Magnus] said, ‘Well, we may do something about that.’

“And that’s where the germ of the idea of the Friday show we do was born. I was just blessed to be at the right place at the right time.”

Magnus, as well as other ESPN executives, began to see Pate as a potential personality to fill the college football void at the network, FOS reported in January. The show was officially announced ahead of the 2026 season—less than a year after that fateful lunch in Atlanta.

The post How a Lunch in Atlanta Led to Josh Pate’s ESPN College Football Show appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Josh Pate, John Fanta Blast CFP Expansion: ‘Why Stop at 24?’
item.dc:creator: Kennington Smith III
item.description: The deadline for College Football Playoff expansion in 2027 is Dec. 1, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
There’s growing momentum for an expanded College Football Playoff. Last month, the CFP issued a statement announcing its officially considering expansion to 24 teams, while launching a 30-day negotiating window with ESPN. However, influential media members question if expansion will stop there. 

NBC Sports broadcaster John Fanta and Josh Pate, host of Josh Pate’s College Football Show and contributing analyst at ESPN, slammed the idea of expansion at the Front Office Sports Tuned In summit Tuesday morning. 

“We’re going to call it an expanded playoff,” Pate said. “Really, what it is is it’s an ATM to bail out very bad decision-making from, and I use this term loosely, leadership in college football.” 

The formal deadline for whether the CFP will expand to 24 teams for the 2027 season is on Dec. 1; if an agreement is not reached, then it will remain at 12 teams next season. 

Fanta’s seen expansion in another sport he covers: college basketball. The NCAA tournament has expanded from 64 teams to 68 in recent years and will debut a 76-team field this upcoming season. When asked his opinion by Front Office Sports’s Ryan Glasspiegel, he wonders if the CFP will follow a similar trend of continued growth. 

“The effort’s going to be there, the pageantry, the theater of it’s going to be there,” Fanta said. “I get all those things, and I love that about college football. I think college football is really fun, but we have barely given 12 teams time and runway. The moment that it goes to 12, we say 24. When it goes to 24, are we going to try to go to 30?” 

Pate quickly quipped back, adding to Fanta’s point. 

“For all of these reasons that you would expand to 24, I keep looking, and I keep saying, why would you stop at 24?” Pate said. “Why not go to 36? It’s the college basketball effect, but it’s just in college football.” 

The College Football Playoff debuted in 2014 with four teams. The field expanded to 12 teams after the 2023 season and has changed in each subsequent season. 

In 2024, the four highest-ranked conference champions received first-round byes. In 2025, the seeding protocol changed, and the 12 qualifying teams were ranked from highest to lowest. This year, the Power 4 conferences will each be guaranteed a spot for their conference champion, along with one spot for the highest-ranked team from the Group of 6 (formerly the Group of 5). Last season’s ACC champion, Duke, was left out after a 7-5 regular season. 

While comparing the two sports, Fanta acknowledged that expansion in basketball seems more practical than football. The variance in the NCAA tournament over its history lends itself to more upsets and parity. Conversely, the average margin of victory in the first round of College Football Playoff games in the first two years of the 12-team era has been nearly 18 points per game. 

“Basketball is different than football. It just is,” Fanta said. “You can come out, and you can go 10 for your first 13 from (three-point range) and be involved in the game. In college football, the game is won and lost in the trenches, and we’re seeing it in a lot of these first-round college football playoff games.

“I don’t think there’s nearly as much of a difference between (the 75th team and the 55th team) in college basketball. There’s a difference in college football, a significant one.” 

Despite public criticisms, industry leaders feel a 24-team CFP is inevitable at some point. More than expanded access and parity, Pate believes the idea is being pushed through to increase revenue and viewership. 

“The movers in college football are even going so far as to acknowledge publicly, ‘We know that fan support, or sentiment rather, is against this,” Pate said. “It’s almost that ‘Well, you’ll watch anyway’. You know, you’ll take what we give you anyway. But in the aggregate, we’ve really screwed this up nine ways from Sunday. We need a bailout. We’ve got to create revenue somewhere.”

The post Josh Pate, John Fanta Blast CFP Expansion: ‘Why Stop at 24?’ appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: WNBA Moves Finals Dates So Dream Can Play in NBA Arena
item.dc:creator: Colin Salao
item.description: Game 3 was moved up a day.
item.content:encoded:
The WNBA has rescheduled Games 3 and 4 of the Finals, allowing the Atlanta Dream to host their games at the 17,000-seat State Farm Arena, the league announced Tuesday.

Game 3 has been moved to Wednesday, Oct. 21, a day before the game’s original date. The game originally overlapped with a Sombr concert at State Farm Arena.

Game 4 will still be played on its original date—Saturday, Oct. 24—but it will be adjusted from 3:30 p.m. ET to 1 p.m. The NBA’s Hawks play their home opener at 8:30 p.m. ET on the same date, though the game’s tip-off time was moved from 8 p.m.

The Hawks operate State Farm Arena, which is owned by the Atlanta Fulton County Recreation Authority, and have played there since it opened in 1999.

Front Office Sports reported before the announcement that the league was heavily considering changing its Finals schedule.

The league has not announced a decision on Game 6, which will be played in Atlanta if necessary. 

The Dream have played their first- and second-round playoff games at State Farm Arena, averaging nearly 10,000 fans per game over three games. A Dream spokesperson told FOS last week that the team has limited attendance in its upper bowl due to the short turnaround to sell playoff tickets.

The Dream played six regular-season games at State Farm Arena, selling out the full 17,000-seat venue five times. But the team played the majority of its regular-season games at the 3,500-seat Gateway Center, their home arena since 2021.

Because of the schedule conflict, the Dream were expected to host Finals games at Gateway Center.

A change in the date will also impact the WNBA Finals broadcast partners. NBC will air Games 1 and 4, while USA Network will air Games 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7. 

Game 3 of the WNBA Finals was originally scheduled to face off against a Thursday Night Football game between the Bears and Patriots. The move to Wednesday, Oct. 21 gives it a free spot on the calendar, with the World Series set to begin Oct. 23.

The post WNBA Moves Finals Dates So Dream Can Play in NBA Arena appeared first on Front Office Sports.

item.title: Controversial Search Firm Memo on Brian Flores Unsealed by Court
item.dc:creator: Daniel Kaplan
item.description: The memo is evidence for several of Flores's claims, his lawyers say.
item.content:encoded:
The controversial Brian Flores memo prepared by recruiter Korn Ferry for the Las Vegas Raiders for one of their recent head coaching hiring cycles was unsealed Tuesday morning.

Through his lawyers, Flores—who is suing the NFL and six teams for racial discrimination—has called this memo proof of his claims against the NFL. But it had been under seal until Tuesday.

The most charged section of the one-page memo is likely the following:

“Polished and a good presenter despite growing up in Brownsville, Brooklyn (same as Mike Tyson). He was able to build a strong friendship with a billionaire’s son which gave him opportunities to socialize and learn how to build relationships with white-collar and upper-class individuals.” 

That paragraph is contained in a page that lists six points in favor of Flores, and seven points against (the above is on the positive side).  On the negative side, Korn Ferry writes, “He can fool you with his polish upwards.” His lawyer, Michael Willemin, told Front Office Sports that the comment is a “racially offensive way in which someone might comment upon a Black man being articulate, as though it is surprising for a Black man to be articulate (or, in this case, polished).” 

And the Brownsville reference, he said, infers that the only reason someone from Brownsville—which is 81% Black and Hispanic—could succeed is if he met a billionaire’s son.

“The recently unsealed documents demonstrate two unfortunate, but unsurprising, realities,” Flores attorney Douglas H. Wigdor said in a statement to FOS. “First, that Mr. Flores’ decision to hold the league and its teams accountable for systemic race discrimination has been met with unlawful retaliation. Second, discrimination continues to play a significant role in the hiring process for NFL Head Coaches, as evidenced by the fact that the candidate profile prepared for the Raiders leans heavily on racial stereotypes. We and Mr. Flores are committed to eradicating the institutional racism and retaliation that permeates the league, its teams and their partners.”

Willemin, speaking to FOS, points to the last negative listed by Korn Ferry—that the lawsuit, filed in 2022, might be a distraction—as evidence of retaliation. (Flores has had a highly successful tenure as Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator since filing the suit.)

Among the other negative points: 

“Chip on his shoulder – can be a dictator with players, coaches, and can even be difficult with ownership. His personality is unpredictable – not sure who is going to show up. Failed in how he hires coordinators and staff because he doesn’t give second chances or see efforts to improve; Needs someone strong at the top to reign in some of his worst behavior. He once threatened violence to his GM and made irrational demands during an ownership meeting. One long-time senior team executive said, ‘He may have changed since, but he was the worst hiring decision we’ve ever made.’ Another President of a club refused to talk about him.” 

Willemin told FOS these descriptions conjure up the image of the “angry Black man.” (Flores’s parents immigrated to the United States from Honduras.)

One allegation that Flores has made against the Miami Dolphins, which employed him as head coach for three seasons until 2021, is that the team defamed him. If the quote about him being the worst hiring decision is from a Miami executive, that could be the basis of the defamation claim.

Korn Ferry sought to keep the memo sealed, arguing it is a third party to the lawsuit, the memo is a privileged work product, and the memo doesn’t say what Flores claims in any event. Those defenses were rejected by the magistrate judge overseeing the discovery process of the case, and Korn Ferry did not appeal to the district judge.

Flores filed his suit on Feb. 1, 2022, and added former head coaches Steve Wilks and Ray Horton as plaintiffs several months later. However, for much of the time since, the case was consumed by venue issues: whether the case belonged in court or arbitration. Ultimately the case ended up in court; three of the teams have an appeal still pending. The next legal marker will be the judge’s decisions on motions to dismiss.

The six teams are the Dolphins, Denver Broncos, New York Giants, Houston Texans, Arizona Cardinals, and Tennessee Titans. The Broncos, Giants, and Texans are sued for not hiring Flores. The Titans are named for allegedly giving Horton a sham interview for head coach. Wilks’s claim against the Cardinals is over his short tenure as head coach there. 

The post Controversial Search Firm Memo on Brian Flores Unsealed by Court appeared first on Front Office Sports.
